data.name: 40 Days [四十天]
data.detailed_description:
40 Days is a special strategy simulation game related to infectious diseases spread all over the city. You, as ahead of quarantine department, have been given full authority and manpower to contain the city, deal with different parties, virus in the city and most importantly find out the cure.

Main Objective
  • Find the Cure within 40 days

  • Choose wisely


Key Features
  • Take action like Air Drop, Reinforcement. Examine Citizen, Send Infect to Lab and so on
  • Virus research and face the virus mutant
  • Maintain the medicine price
  • Deal with medicine business man
  • Depress the cult
  • Manage your city
  • Manage your lab
  • Make decision during Critical Moment
  • Make decision during random events
  • Face the Vigilante
  • Defend attack wave from Angry Mob
  • Protect your facilities
  • Upgrade your base

reviews.review:
40 Days takes the familiar concept of a deadly epidemic and approaches it from the perspective of the people responsible for containing the disaster. Developed and published by Black Phoenix Studio, it is a strategy and management game in which the player takes command of a quarantine department during a rapidly worsening outbreak. The central challenge is immediately understandable: there are only forty days to research the disease, develop a cure, and prevent the city from collapsing. That fixed deadline gives the campaign its identity, turning time into one of the most important resources available.

The gameplay is built around managing several interconnected problems rather than simply waiting for researchers to discover a solution. Laboratory work is essential, and infected citizens or useful samples must be examined to improve understanding of the virus. The disease can mutate, making research an ongoing struggle rather than a completely predictable progression toward victory. Every day spent improving the scientific response is also another day in which infection, shortages, disorder, or other emergencies can become more dangerous. This creates a constant tension between solving immediate problems and investing in the cure required to win the campaign.

Resource management adds another layer of pressure. Players can arrange air drops and reinforcements, manage medicine, upgrade their base, and decide how limited resources should be distributed. Medicine also has an economic dimension, with pricing and interactions involving medicine businessmen becoming part of the overall situation. These mechanics help communicate that an epidemic affects much more than hospitals. Public health, commerce, logistics, security, and scientific research are all competing for attention, forcing the player to determine which problems deserve priority.

The city itself can become increasingly unstable as the crisis develops. Angry mobs may attack important locations, while vigilantes and cult activity create additional threats that cannot simply be solved in the laboratory. Protecting facilities and maintaining order therefore become important parts of surviving the forty days. This gives the game an unusual character because the enemy is not merely the virus. Fear, social unrest, opportunism, and failing infrastructure can become equally serious obstacles. The concept is ambitious for a relatively modest strategy game and produces some genuinely tense situations when several emergencies appear close together.

Random events and critical decisions make planning less predictable. A carefully organized strategy can suddenly require adjustment when an unexpected situation consumes resources or creates a new threat. This unpredictability improves replayability because campaigns do not necessarily unfold in exactly the same manner. It also means that players need to remain flexible rather than relying on a single optimized routine. The downside is that unfavorable events can sometimes make an already difficult campaign feel excessively punishing, particularly before the player understands which resources and upgrades are most valuable.

Base development provides a useful sense of progression throughout the campaign. Upgrading facilities can strengthen the quarantine operation and improve the player's ability to deal with later problems, but investing too heavily in long-term improvements can leave the city vulnerable in the present. This creates one of the game's better strategic dilemmas. Resources spent preparing for tomorrow cannot necessarily solve today's emergency, while repeatedly choosing short-term solutions can result in an operation that is poorly equipped for the more serious stages of the outbreak.

The forty-day structure keeps the experience focused but also contributes heavily to its difficulty. There is little room for careless experimentation once a campaign is underway. Research, medicine, infection control, security, economic considerations, facility upgrades, reinforcements, and unpredictable events can all demand attention simultaneously. Failure is therefore part of learning the game. Players who enjoy gradually discovering effective management strategies may appreciate this structure, while those who prefer relaxed city building or extensive opportunities to recover from mistakes may find it frustrating.

Presentation is comparatively modest, with functionality taking priority over spectacle. The game relies primarily on its management systems and strategic decisions to create tension rather than elaborate graphics or cinematic storytelling. Its interface and overall production values can feel rough compared with larger strategy titles, and some systems would benefit from clearer explanations and greater mechanical depth. Even so, the limited presentation does not undermine the central idea. Watching an outbreak evolve while attempting to keep multiple systems functioning provides enough pressure to support the game's atmosphere.

Steam Deck compatibility is uncertain from an official standpoint, as the game does not have a clearly established Steam Deck Verified or Playable designation. Its interface-oriented design and older PC-focused controls also mean that handheld play should not automatically be expected to provide an ideal experience. It may be possible to run the game through Steam Deck's compatibility environment, but players should be prepared for potential control, interface, or configuration adjustments rather than treating it as a fully supported Deck title.

Ultimately, 40 Days is an interesting but imperfect attempt to turn epidemic containment into a compact strategic crisis. Its strongest quality is the way it combines research, mutations, medicine management, economic concerns, base development, public disorder, hostile groups, random incidents, and a strict deadline into one continuously escalating situation. Some mechanics lack the refinement necessary to fulfill the concept's full potential, and the difficulty can occasionally work against accessibility. Nevertheless, players who enjoy demanding management games and unusual simulation concepts may find the challenge rewarding, especially when a seemingly doomed campaign is finally brought under control through careful planning.

Rating: 6/10
